Adamjee Jute Mills Limited, represented by its Executive Director & anr ----- Petitioner
Vs
Chairman, Third Labour Court, Dhaka and another ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
Kazi Ebadul Hoque J: This Rule was issued at the instance of the petitioners Adamjee Jute Mills and its Deputy General Manager calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why judgment and decision dated 4-9-95 passed by the respondent No.1 in Complaint Case No. 19/1993 should not be declared to have been passed without any lawful authority and of no legal effect. 

 2. Learned Advocate for the petitioners after placing the impugned judgment and other materials on record submitted that by the impugned judgment IRO Case No. 43 of 1989 and Complaint Case No. 19 of 1993 has been disposed of dismissing the IRO case and allowing the Complaint Case under misconception of law that during pendency of the IRO Case no order of termination or dismissal could be passed against a worker as provided under section 47 of the Industrial Relations Ordinance. He further submitted that IRO Case in question was not in respect of any industrial dispute and, as such, section 47 had no application during the pendency of the said IRO Case. He also submitted that application under section 25 of the Employment of Labour (Standing) Orders Act was not maintainable against an order of termination simpliciter. 

 3. Learned Advocate for the respondent No. 2 after placing the affidavit-in-opposition and other materials on record submitted that termination in question was not a termination simpliciter but it was a malafide order of dismissal under the garb of dismissal to teach a lesson to the respondent No. 2 for filing the IRO Case. 

 4. It appears that respondent No. 2 filed IRO Case No. 43 of 1987 praying for back wages for one year one month and 4 days between the period of termination and re-instatement in service. During pendency of the said case while respondent No. 3 was on leave with effect from 27-2-93 he was again terminated from service by order dated 13-3-93 with the malafide object of depriving him from getting his arrear salary of Taka 16,120, fringe benefit of Taka 7,592.00 total Taka 23,712.00. Both the cases were contested by the petitioners before the Labour Court. In the IRO Case petitioner's stand was that respondent No. 2 was re-instated in service on condition of his refunding the termination benefit and foregoing the salary for the period from termination and reinstatement treating the said period as leave without pay. Petitioners contention in the complaint case was that respondent No. 2 filed the IRO Case No. 43 of 1989 out of malafide motive on false allegations to harass the petitioners and his service was terminated on 26-2-93 as there was no necessity of his service and he was merely entitled to the termination benefit. By filing an amendment petition petitioners took stand that respondent No. 2 received the termination benefit. 

 5. Labour Court, on consideration of the materials on record, found that the order of termination was malafide order of dismissal in the garb of termination simpliciter and the same was issued during pendency of the IRO Case No. 43 of 1989 to give the respondent No. 2 a lesson for instituting the case and during pendency of the Industrial dispute such action cannot be taken in view  of the provision of section 47 of the Industrial Relations Ordinance though the IRO Case in question did not come within the definition of Industrial dispute in view of provision of section 43 of the said Ordinance and an employer should not be given any licence to frustrate a sub-judice matter purposely terminating the employee on his fancy desire and there was no explanation from the side of the employer as to why the said order of termination was made while the respondent No. 2 was on annual leave. 

 6. It appears from the provisions of section 47 of the Ordinance that the employer shall discharge, dismiss, terminate or otherwise punish any work without the permission of the Labour Court during pendency of proceedings before it in respect of an industrial dispute. Respondent No.2 filed the aforesaid IRO Case No. 43 of 1989 as an individual worker only for payment of back wages and not a Collective Bargaining Agent in respect of any industrial dispute and, as such, section 47 of the Ordinance has no manner of application in the case of termination of the respondent No. 2. It appears from the impugned judgment that Labour Court is quite aware of the same and correctly opined that IRO Case No. 43 of 1989 did not come within the definition of an industrial dispute under section 47 of the said Ordinance. But it held by analogy that during pendency of a case employer should not be allowed to Lake action against workman to frustrate sub-judice matter. On going though the provisions of sections 43 and 47 of the said Ordinance along with other provisions of the said Ordinance and facts and circumstances of the case we find merit in the contention of the learned Advocate for the petitioners that IRO Case filed by the respondent No. 2 as an individual worker cannot debar the employer from terminating his service during pendency of such a case. 

 7. Labour Court on consideration of the materials on record found that though no complaint case lies against an order or termination simpliciter such a case be entertained when a worker is dismissed from service in a malafide manner in the garb of termination simpliciter. From the facts and circumstances of the case, materials on record specially averment of the petitioners and written statement filed in the complaint case No. 19 of 1993 stating that respondent No. 2 filed IRO Case No. 43 of 1989 with malafide intention with false and baseless allegations to harass them, it is difficult to disagree with the Labour Court that the respondent No. 2 was, in fact, dismissed from service in the garb of a termination simpliciter. Labour Court was well conscious that bar under section 47 of the Ordinance was not applicable in the case but opined that the principles under that section should be applied in the instant case. The employer cannot be allowed to frustrate a sub-judice matter in terminating the worker only on its fancy desire specially when he is enjoying leave.
